description_full: Rio Tinto Group engages in exploring, mining, and processing mineral resources worldwide. The company operates through Iron Ore; Aluminium and lithium; and Copper segments. The Iron Ore segment engages in the iron ore mining, and salt and gypsum production in Western Australia. The Aluminum and lithium segment is involved in bauxite mining; alumina refining; and aluminium smelting, and recycling, as well as mining and processing of lithium. The Copper segment engages in mining and refining of copper, gold, silver, molybdenum, and other by-products and exploration activities. It also owns and operates open pit and underground mines; and refineries, smelters, processing plants and power, and shipping facilities. The company was founded in 1873 and is headquartered in London, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: Rio Tinto Ltd. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $168.4B market cap on $57.6B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are contracting by -2.7pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 8% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 59% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $4.5B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.69× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.4×.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 5.3% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 27% operating margin runs 17pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.06x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 3.4% of sector revenue and 7.1% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 30% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 18% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 23% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 45% and a beta of 0.67, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.16 vs 5y 0.52), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $39K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 40% in the 2020 crash and 37% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $92.87 (margin of safety -11%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 9%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $67.85 to $129 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/FCF 37.4 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 2.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 7.3% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.20).
It runs a 59% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.69x.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.7x net debt to EBITDA ($7.5B of cash against $23.5B of debt), with interest covered 8.4x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.2% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 46% of profits supports about 8.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own 5.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 65%.
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (4.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years.
people: With about 56,890 employees, each generates about $1.0M of revenue, 1.6x the Basic Materials median.
That works out to $79K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.4M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
